prompt:
Write the lyrics of a folk song about a river being dammed.

Write it as a working songwriter would, to be sung: lines that scan against a steady beat, a chorus that earns its repetition by meaning something slightly different each time it comes back, and verses that move a story forward through particular scenes, names, brands and street-level detail. Say the thing sideways: no line that states the feeling outright, no stock phrases, no word chosen only because it rhymes. Put one detail in each verse that only this story could contain.

Output only the lyrics, as plain lines with a blank line between sections: no title, no section labels, no chords, no commentary.
raw:
Wes Miller drove a tanker truck for the county asphalt plant
Carried a Thermos of black coffee and a notebook in his pants
He wrote down every mend and turn the old Two-Ribbon made
In ’68 the surveyors came and numbered every page

And the water don’t sing like it sang before
It don’t remember what it sang for
You can hear it at night if you hold your mouth just right
But it’s not a song you’d want to dance to anymore

Stone & Webster brought the batch plant in on fourteen flatbed cars
My uncle faked a bad back just to get up close and watch
They poured the spillway in one pour—thirty-seven hours straight
He said the coffee came in cups that said “Del Webb, est. 1928”

And the water don’t sing like it sang before
It don’t remember what it sang for
You can hear it at night if you hold your mouth just right
But it’s not a song you’d want to dance to anymore

The Wilson place went under first—you could see the hayloft door
Marlene Wilson hung a bedsheet out that read “See You On The Shore”
The county bought the graves up from the Baptist church on Route 9
They rest now on the high ground where the sun hits through the pines

The water don’t sing like it sang before
It don’t remember what it sang for
You can hear it at night if you hold your mouth just right
But it’s not a song you’d want to dance to anymore

Now the bassboat men in polar fleece come idling out at dawn
They’re fishing for a Wal-Mart state-record striped or maybe not
It’s glassy when the wind is dead and still as a machine
A heron stands on one damp leg like a question no one needs

And the water don’t sing like it sang before
It don’t remember what it sang for
You can hear it at night if you hold your mouth just right
But it’s not a song you’d want to dance to anymore
